pr_body:
Fix #45651. The bug happens when a synchronous `ReceiveFrom` is being used after asynchronous `SendToAsync` call(s) on the same socket. As @tmds pointed out in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/45651#issuecomment-744637362, we did not set `SetReceiveFlags = true` in `SocketAsyncContext.ReceiveFrom`
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/31062e4ec6b248b709095e13947400b49d507e53/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/SocketAsyncContext.Unix.cs#L1510-L1516

which resulted in `BufferedMemoryReceieveOperation` completion attempt with `recv` instead of `recvmsg`:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/31062e4ec6b248b709095e13947400b49d507e53/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/SocketAsyncContext.Unix.cs#L473-L479

Our existing UDP tests (`SendToRecvFrom_Datagram_UDP`) did not exercise `BufferMemoryReceiveOperation`, because completion of the synchronous `ReceiveFrom` always happened without the use of `_receiveQueue`:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/31062e4ec6b248b709095e13947400b49d507e53/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/SocketAsyncContext.Unix.cs#L1505-L1508

For reasons I don't understand, the `BufferMemoryReceiveOperation` path gets only executed if a synchronous `ReceiveFrom` is being called after an asynchronous operation. The PR adds tests for that case for multiple async variants.
Another weird thing: while my standalone repro resulted in in an assertion failure (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/45651#issuecomment-744631080), the new tests timeout (hang?) instead. (Both issues are fixed with `SetReceiveFlags = true`.)

We should probably consider adding similar tests for TCP send/receive.

@tmds @geoffkizer please take a look. Note: starting from tomorrow, I will be on vacation until the 4th of January, looking at GitHub occasionally.

> For reasons I don't understand, the BufferMemoryReceiveOperation path gets only executed if a synchronous ReceiveFrom is being called after an asynchronous operation. The PR adds tests for that case for multiple async variants.

This is the "sync-over-async" path in SocketAsyncContext.

What happens is this: The OS socket starts out in blocking mode. If you only perform sync IO, it will stay in blocking mode. But as soon as you perform an async IO, we need to switch to nonblocking mode at the OS level. But we still support performing sync operations, even though the underlying OS socket is nonblocking. We do this by simulating sync operations on top of the async infrastructure in SocketAsyncContext. So the sync caller will block on a ManualResetEventSlim that we signal when the operation can proceed, and from the user's point of view this looks and behaves like sync IO, even though under the covers it actually is done using a nonblocking socket and epoll.

We do have a bunch of tests for this. See `SocketHelperSyncForceNonBlocking`. _(Edit: ignore the following, it's incorrect. Unfortunately, it seems that these tests only use the sync overloads that take byte[], not the ones that take Memory. We should probably add another case here.__

Edit to add: The problem here seems to be that `SocketHelperSyncForceNonBlocking` doesn't work with UDP; it relies on hooking the Connect and Accept methods to force the socket to be nonblocking. We should fix this, perhaps by just adding explicit calls to SocketTestExtensions.ForceNonBlocking in the UDP tests.
@geoffkizer `ForceNonBlocking` seems to be sufficient to reproduce the issue. I pushed a change that applies it with the help of `SocketTestHelper`, PTAL.
Are there other UDP tests that should be calling ConfigureNonBlocking? Seems like there must be.
I was only able to find one more among the generic tests utilizing the SocketTestHelper infrastructure (`UdpReceiveGetsCanceledByDispose`), pushed a change for that.

issue_context.title: Socket ReceiveFrom() and SendTo() issues on Linux after .NET 5 upgrade
issue_context.body:
<!--This is just a template - feel free to delete any and all of it and replace as appropriate.-->

### Description
An open source DNS server project that I am working currently uses .NET 3.1 and works well on Linux and Windows. I upgraded the project to .NET 5 and it stop functioning immediately without any kind of errors being generated. So I started investigating the issue and used Console.WriteLine and tcpdump on capture packets on all networks on the Ubuntu 20.04 VM.

### Configuration

* The code is running .NET 5. Earlier the same code worked perfectly on .NET 3.1.
* Tested on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS x64.
* OS is running in a VM with 1 CPU and 1GB RAM.

### Regression?

From the investigations, it seems there is an issue with how Socket handles ReceiveFrom() and SendTo() in .NET 5 upgrade. The ReceiveFrom() is giving wrong `remoteEP` values after a couple of packets. The remoteEP values keep on repeating in the Console.WriteLine() which meant that the method is giving wrong EndPoint for the received packet.

Further more, the SendTo() method sends the packets to a `remoteEP` different from the one provided in the argument. It too seems to gets stuck on the same end point after sending a couple of packets and then keeps on sending packets to destination that was not specified in the `remoteEP` argument.

This issue comes only on Linux and Windows seems to be not affected.

### Other information

Attaching PCAP files to inspect in a zip file: [dns-issue-pcap.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/files/5648857/dns-issue-pcap.zip)

1. `dns-issue1.pcap` : In here ICMP port unreachable can be observed as the DNS server responds to a request with the stuck end point "127.0.0.1:36145". Expected destination end point is "192.168.180.1:54290" for the last response in the pcap.

2. `dns-issue2.pcap`: In here the DNS server is sending response to a stuck end point where the IP seems to be correct but the port number is different ie. "192.168.180.1:58002". Expected destination end point is "192.168.180.1:62807" for the last response in the pcap.

The link to the affected DNS server project code to show the .NET 3.1 working implementation that broke with .NET 5 upgrade: https://github.com/TechnitiumSoftware/DnsServer/blob/master/DnsServerCore/Dns/DnsServer.cs#L224-L354

@ShreyasZare can you provide a small reproducer?

Thanks for the replies. I have create a small dns proxy app that can reproduce this issue on .NET 5 on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.

Here is the link to the repo: [https://github.com/ShreyasZare/DnsProxy](https://github.com/ShreyasZare/DnsProxy)

While I created and tested this app, it was noticed that the code works well when SendTo() is used but actually fails when async call BeginSendTo() is being used.

Dotnet version installed on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS: `Microsoft.NETCore.App 5.0.0 [/opt/dotnet/shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App]`

Steps to reproduce the issue:
1. Copy and run the project output in ubuntu machine with .NET 5.0.0 installed: `dotnet DnsProxy.dll`
2. Use `nslookup www.google.com <ip-address>` to query the app. Where `<ip-address>` is the IP address of the ubuntu machine. If on the same machine use loopback (127.0.0.1) address.
3. You will notice that `nslookup` gives request timeout messages as shown below:
```
C:\Users\user>nslookup www.google.com 192.168.180.129
DNS request timed out.
    timeout was 2 seconds.
Server:  UnKnown
Address:  192.168.180.129

DNS request timed out.
    timeout was 2 seconds.
DNS request timed out.
    timeout was 2 seconds.
DNS request timed out.
    timeout was 2 seconds.
DNS request timed out.
    timeout was 2 seconds.
*** Request to UnKnown timed-out
```
4. Repeat the same experiment on Windows with .NET 5 installed and you will notice that `nslookup` returns response as expected.

Observations:
1. The dns proxy app's console output will look as shown below. The end point address that is printed remains same as that of the remote end point of the first UDP packet that was received. The app keeps transmitting responses to this stuck end point that ReceiveFrom() keeps returning for each subsequent packet.
```
DNS proxy is running. Press CTRL+C to terminate.
ReceiveFrom: 192.168.180.1:64816
SendTo: 192.168.180.1:64816
ReceiveFrom: 192.168.180.1:64816
SendTo: 192.168.180.1:64816
ReceiveFrom: 192.168.180.1:64816

ReceiveFrom: 192.168.180.1:64816
SendTo: 192.168.180.1:64816
ReceiveFrom: 192.168.180.1:64816
SendTo: 192.168.180.1:64816
ReceiveFrom: 192.168.180.1:64816
SendTo: 192.168.180.1:64816
ReceiveFrom: 192.168.180.1:64816
SendTo: 192.168.180.1:64816
ReceiveFrom: 192.168.180.1:64816
SendTo: 192.168.180.1:64816
```
2. When `nslookup` is tested from the same ubuntu console then the following output is seen. In here the loopback endpoint gets stuck and when `nslookup` query is made from another computer on the network, the app sends UDP responses to the stuck loopback end point. These responses can be seen if you run tcpdump and observe the output which is similar to the pcap that were provided earlier.
```
DNS proxy is running. Press CTRL+C to terminate.
ReceiveFrom: 127.0.0.1:56960
SendTo: 127.0.0.1:56960
ReceiveFrom: 127.0.0.1:56960
SendTo: 127.0.0.1:56960

ReceiveFrom: 127.0.0.1:56960
SendTo: 127.0.0.1:56960
ReceiveFrom: 127.0.0.1:56960
SendTo: 127.0.0.1:56960
ReceiveFrom: 127.0.0.1:56960
SendTo: 127.0.0.1:56960
ReceiveFrom: 127.0.0.1:56960
SendTo: 127.0.0.1:56960
```

The code in question in marked here to inspect: [https://github.com/ShreyasZare/DnsProxy/blob/master/DnsProxy/DnsProxyService.cs#L54-L62](https://github.com/ShreyasZare/DnsProxy/blob/master/DnsProxy/DnsProxyService.cs#L54-L62)

There are 3 ways tried to send response. You can test each one by commenting the other. The first one that uses SendTo() blocking call works as expected but the other two fail.

The other two calls however work on Windows with .NET 5 and work for both Windows and Linux with .NET Core 3.1.

This issue does not occur when using ReceiveFromAsync() with SendToAsync() and thus updating my code to use ReceiveFromAsync(). 

This change also improves the performance on top of already significant performance improvements from moving to .NET 5 by itself.

Removing the caching of the `LocalEndpoint` doesn't help. With Debug builds we end up with an assertion failure in `SocketAsyncContext.Unix`:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/31062e4ec6b248b709095e13947400b49d507e53/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/SocketAsyncContext.Unix.cs#L475

The assertion keeps failing when switching from `ReceiveFrom` to `ReceiveFromAsync` as suggested in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/45651#issuecomment-744010117.

Might be a side effect of the .NET 5 performance refactors.
@antonfirsov, since you can reproduce the issue, can you check if https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/45683 has an effect?

I think we are missing `SetReceivedFlags = true` here:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/31062e4ec6b248b709095e13947400b49d507e53/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/SocketAsyncContext.Unix.cs#L1510-L1516
@tmds yeah `SetReceivedFlags = true` seems to fix the issue. Will raise a PR tomorrow.
I wonder why tests haven't caught this.

> I wonder why tests haven't caught this.

+1. I assume we just don't have tests for this particular combination (async ReceiveFrom with Memory) or something like that, but it's still concerning.

I want to produce a minimal repro and add a new test to the PR. It has probably something to do with `SendTo` & `ReceiveFrom` happening from the same socket which is not exercised by our current UDP tests.

Unfortunately some new (?) infra changes seemingly broke my entire Linux workflow, I'm not sure anymore if I can finish the troubleshooting and do any meaningful progress before my vacation.
Reopening until the fix gets backported.
Fixed in 5.0.3 in PR #46629 and in 6.0 (master) in PR #46151
